name: John Fothergill
bio: Architect-trained aesthete, art dealer and later celebrated innkeeper; per Sox the one member of E. P. Warren's Lewes House brotherhood to become well known in Britain. Born 27 February 1876, son of George Fothergill of a fairly well-off Westmorland family; met Wilde at 19 through Robbie Ross and Reggie Turner, put in brief stints at the London School of Architecture (a pupil of architecture at 30 Manchester Street, 'to be near Sir Arthur Blomfield') and the Slade School of Art, dabbled in classical archaeology, and managed the Carfax Gallery. Wilde inscribed Fothergill's copy of The Ballad of Reading Gaol 'To Rowland Fothergill, the Architect of the Moon'. Ran the Spreadeagle at Thame near Oxford as innkeeper-author - the innkeeping diaries published in the 1930s and 1940s made his name - and died in a modest terraced house in Rugby on 26 April 1957, aged 81.
bio_note: All facts read in the source 2026-08-03 in Sox (1991). Introduction printed pp. vii-viii (PDF 11-12, roman-folio offset +4): died 26 April 1957 in Rugby aged 81; 'dabbled in classical archaeology, put in brief stints studying at the London School of Architecture and the Slade School of Art, and managed the Carfax Gallery'; 'the one member of the Lewes House brotherhood to become well known in Britain'. P. 133 (PDF 149): born 27 February 1876, son of George Fothergill, 'fairly well-off Westmorland family'; full name John Rowland Fothergill, called Rowland by some friends and Roland or Ronald by others; innkeeping diaries of the 1930s-1940s. P. 137 (PDF 153): met Wilde at 19 through Ross and Reggie Turner. P. 138 (PDF 154): architecture pupil at 30 Manchester Street near Blomfield; the Ballad inscription. Sox's caveat on his main source (p. 133): Fothergill's unpublished 81-page memoir (written 1954, three years before his death) is unfinished, 'highly disorganized', with 'few dates given'. Warren bond NOT entered under context_engagements: in pages read so far Sox says only that Fothergill had 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142) - no explicit romantic/sexual characterization read in the source.
